paragraphs.context: I have long wanted to send Jack and Annie to China
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the writer found the idea for this book.
paragraphs.simple: The writer wanted to send Jack and Annie to China, but she did not know which time in history to choose. Then in a library she found out about a great discovery: an old tomb with more than 7,000 statues of soldiers and horses, made for the first emperor of China over 2,000 years ago.

background.note: In 1974, farmers digging a well near the city of Xi'an in China found pieces of clay soldiers. This was the start of the discovery of the famous Terracotta Army.
The first emperor of China was Qin Shi Huang (in this book "Shi Huangdi"). He made China one country in 221 B.C.

paragraphs.context: After I learned this, I found other library books
paragraphs.mainIdea: She read many books and made this story from her notes.
paragraphs.simple: She read more library books about that time in Chinese history and took notes for days. Then she used her notes to make (write) this book.

paragraphs.context: Have I told you before that libraries are very important to me?
paragraphs.mainIdea: Libraries are magic places for the writer.

paragraphs.tone: Warm and friendly, like a letter to a friend.

paragraphs.mainIdea: She hopes readers will visit their library too.
paragraphs.simple: She tells readers to go to their own library. She is sure they will find the same magic there.

paragraphs.context: One summer day in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania
paragraphs.simple: One summer a strange, magic tree house appeared in the woods near Jack and Annie's home in the town of Frog Creek.

background.note: Pennsylvania is a state in the east of the United States. Frog Creek is a made-up town there.

paragraphs.context: Eight-year-old Jack and his seven-year-old sister
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie found the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack, who is eight, and his sister Annie, who is seven, climbed up into the tree house. It was full of books.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie soon discovered that the tree house was magic.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house can take them into the pictures in books.
paragraphs.simple: They learned that the tree house was magic. If they pointed to a picture in a book and wished to go there, the tree house took them to that place.

paragraphs.context: Along the way, they discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: On their trips they learned that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay. She is a magic librarian from the time of King Arthur. She travels through time and collects books.

background.note: In the old stories about King Arthur, Morgan le Fay is a woman with magic powers. In these books she is a kind, magic librarian.
King Arthur is a king in very old British stories. He and his knights lived in the castle of Camelot.

paragraphs.context: In Magic Tree House #12, Polar Bears Past Bedtime
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack and Annie became Master Librarians.
paragraphs.simple: In Book 12 they answered the last of four old riddles and became Master Librarians. Morgan gave them secret library cards with the letters M L on them.

background.note: Book 12 of the series. Jack and Annie travel to the Arctic, the cold land around the North Pole.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie’s first four missions as Master Librarians
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their missions are to save stories from old libraries.
paragraphs.simple: As Master Librarians, their first four jobs are to save stories from ancient libraries. After their first trip, to Pompeii in Book 13, Morgan asked them to come back in two weeks to go to China.

background.note: Book 13 of the series. Jack and Annie go to the Roman town of Pompeii just before the volcano Mount Vesuvius erupts.

paragraphs.context: Now the two weeks are over
paragraphs.simple: The two weeks have ended. It is time for the next adventure.

paragraphs.context: Annie peeked into Jack’s room.
paragraphs.simple: Annie looked quickly into Jack's room and asked if he was ready to go to China.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply, because he was a little nervous, and said "Sure".

paragraphs.context: “Bring your secret library card,” Annie said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie reminds Jack about the card.
paragraphs.simple: Annie tells Jack to bring his secret library card. She has hers in her pocket.

paragraphs.context: He opened his top dresser drawer and took out a thin wooden card.
paragraphs.simple: Jack took his wooden library card out of a drawer. The letters M L shone in the light. He put the card, his notebook and a pencil into his backpack.

background.note: M L stands for "Master Librarian".

paragraphs.context: What are we in for today? he wondered.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks: "What will happen to us today?" He is a little worried.

paragraphs.context: “Great,” said their mom. She winked at them.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their mom thinks it is a game.
paragraphs.simple: Their mother thinks Annie is only playing a game, so she winks and says "Have fun."
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Mom does not know the trip is real.

paragraphs.context: Fun? thought Jack. He was afraid that fun wasn’t quite the right word.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks "fun" is not the right word, because their trips are often scary.

paragraphs.context: “Just wish us luck,” he said
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks his mother to say "good luck" to them as they leave the house.

paragraphs.context: “If only she knew we aren’t pretending,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mom does not know the truth.
paragraphs.simple: Jack whispers that he wishes their mother knew that they are not playing a game. Their trips are real.

paragraphs.context: Outside, the sun shone brightly.
paragraphs.simple: It is a sunny day. Birds sing and crickets make high sounds as Jack and Annie walk to the woods.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know. Remember, Morgan said this would be a very scary adventure,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack reminds Annie that Morgan said this trip would be very scary.

paragraphs.context: “They’re always scary,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the trips are always scary, but animals or people always help them.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. He was starting to feel excited now instead of scared.
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiles. Now he feels excited, not afraid.

paragraphs.context: They ran into the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.simple: They run into the woods and go between the tall trees to the big oak tree with the tree house.

paragraphs.context: They looked up. Morgan was peering down from the magic tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan is looking down at them from the tree house window.

paragraphs.context: “Indeed,” said Morgan. “You’re going to ancient China.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says yes, they are going to ancient China. She will show them the title of the story they must find.

paragraphs.context: She held up a long, thin strip of wood.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The title is on a bamboo strip.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan holds up a long, thin piece of wood. It looks like a ruler, but it has Chinese writing on it, not numbers.

paragraphs.context: “Long ago, the Chinese discovered how to make paper.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Books were written on bamboo strips before paper.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the Chinese invented paper, one of the most important discoveries in the world. But Jack and Annie are going to an earlier time, when books were written on bamboo strips.

background.note: Paper was invented in China. A man called Cai Lun made paper better in about A.D. 105, more than 300 years after the time of this story.
Before paper, Chinese books were written with a brush and ink on thin strips of bamboo. The strips were tied together with string and rolled up.

paragraphs.context: “Wow,” said Annie, pointing at the figures on the bamboo.
paragraphs.simple: Annie points at the signs on the bamboo strip and asks if this is Chinese writing.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Morgan. “Just as we have letters
paragraphs.mainIdea: Their job: find the first writing of an old legend.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan explains that Chinese writing uses characters, and each character means a thing or an idea. The characters on the strip are the title of an old Chinese legend. They must find the first copy of it before the emperor's library is destroyed.

background.note: English uses 26 letters to spell words. Chinese uses thousands of characters, and each one has its own meaning.

paragraphs.context: From the folds of her robe, she pulled out a book.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives them a research book.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan takes a book out of her robe. It is called The Time of the First Emperor.

paragraphs.context: “This research book will guide you,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says the book will help them. But when they are in the worst danger, only the old legend can save them.
paragraphs.tone: Mysterious: it is a clue for later.

paragraphs.context: She handed Jack the bamboo strip, and he slipped it into his pack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack puts the strip in his pack.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan gives Jack the bamboo strip, and he puts it into his backpack quickly.

paragraphs.context: Jack pushed his glasses into place, then pointed at the cover of their research book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pushes his glasses up, points at the picture on the book and wishes to go there.

paragraphs.context: The tree house started to spin. It spun faster and faster.
paragraphs.simple: The wind blows and the tree house turns round and round, faster and faster.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, wow,” Annie said. “These clothes feel so soft.
paragraphs.simple: Annie loves her new soft clothes. She also has a pocket for her library card.

paragraphs.context: They no longer wore jeans, T-shirts, and sneakers.
paragraphs.simple: Now they wear big, loose trousers, loose shirts, shoes made of straw and round hats, like people in ancient China.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw that his backpack had become a rough cloth sack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack's backpack is now a sack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's backpack has changed into a bag made of rough cloth. His things are inside it.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out, too. The tree house had landed in a lone tree in a sunny field.
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is in a single tree in a sunny field. Cows are eating grass, and a young man is looking after them. There is a farmhouse, and behind it a city with walls around it.

background.note: Cities in ancient China had high walls around them to keep out enemies. The gates were closed at night.

paragraphs.context: “You can never be sure,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says a place can look peaceful but be dangerous. Pompeii looked peaceful before the volcano erupted.

background.note: Pompeii was the Roman town that Jack and Annie visited in Book 13. A volcano buried it in A.D. 79.

paragraphs.context: He reached in the sack and pulled out the China book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes the China book out of the sack, opens it and reads it aloud.

paragraphs.context: Over 2,000 years ago, China was ruled by its first emperor.
paragraphs.simple: More than 2,000 years ago, the first emperor ruled China. He chose the dragon as his sign, so people called him the Dragon King. In China, dragons are brave and strong.

background.term: dragons are seen as brave and powerful creatures
background.note: In Western stories dragons are often bad and dangerous. In China, dragons are good and strong, and they bring luck and rain. Later, the dragon became the sign of the emperors.

paragraphs.context: Next to the writing was a picture.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A picture of the Dragon King.
paragraphs.simple: The picture shows a man in a long, expensive robe with wide sleeves. He wears a tall hat with beads hanging from it.

background.term: a tall hat with beads hanging from it
background.note: Chinese emperors wore a special hat with strings of beads hanging at the front and back.

paragraphs.context: “The book we need must be in the Dragon King’s library,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the book is in the Dragon King's library, and his palace must be in that walled city.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” he said. “And that’s how to get there.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to a dirt road across the field. It goes to the walled city.

paragraphs.context: Jack threw the China book and his notebook into his sack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts his books in his sack, puts the sack over his shoulder and climbs down after Annie.

paragraphs.context: The man tending the cows was shouting and waving.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The young man runs to them.
paragraphs.simple: The man who looks after the cows shouts, waves and runs toward them.

paragraphs.context: A moment later, the man stood in their path.
paragraphs.simple: The man stands in front of them. He is young, good-looking and has a kind face.

paragraphs.context: “Can you do me a great favor?” he asked.
paragraphs.simple: The man asks them to help him. He says he will be very thankful.

paragraphs.context: “Give a message to the silk weaver.
paragraphs.simple: He asks them to tell the silk weaver at the farmhouse to meet him in the field at twilight, when the sun goes down.

background.note: A silk weaver makes silk cloth on a loom. In this story she is the girl from a famous Chinese legend.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, excuse me—” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks the young man where they can find the Imperial Library.

paragraphs.context: A look of horror crossed the man’s kind face.
paragraphs.simple: For a moment, the man's face shows great fear. He whispers "Why?"

paragraphs.context: “Beware of the Dragon King,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The young man tells them to be very careful of the Dragon King. Then he runs back to his cows.

paragraphs.context: “This place is not as peaceful as it seems,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says this place only looks peaceful. It is really dangerous.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie kept walking across the pasture toward the road.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to give the message.
paragraphs.simple: They walk across the field. When they come near the farmhouse, Annie stops: they must find the silk weaver.

paragraphs.context: “Let’s do that on our way back,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to find the library first.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to give the message later. He is worried about finding the Imperial Library.

paragraphs.context: “What if we don’t have time?” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to keep her promise.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they promised, and the young man was so nice. Maybe they will not have time later.

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” he said. “But let’s find her fast.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agrees. But they must be quick and keep their heads down, so that nobody notices them.

paragraphs.context: As they got closer, Jack peeked out from under his hat.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks out from under his hat. An ox pulls a cart of dry grass. Men dig the ground with hoes. Women push small carts full of grain.

paragraphs.context: “There!” said Annie. She pointed to an open porch
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees a young woman on an open porch. She is making cloth on a loom.

background.note: A loom is a wooden frame for weaving. Threads go up and down on it, and the weaver passes other threads over and under them to make cloth.

paragraphs.context: Annie ran to the silk weaver. Jack looked around to see if anyone was watching.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs to the weaver. Jack looks around, but the farm workers are all busy. He walks carefully to the porch.

paragraphs.context: “What did he say?” the young woman asked.
paragraphs.simple: The weaver asks about the message. Her voice is soft but strong, and her eyes shine with happiness.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, he is.” The silk weaver gave Annie a shy smile.
paragraphs.simple: The weaver smiles shyly. She picks up a ball of yellow thread from a basket near her loom.

paragraphs.context: “It was very brave of you to bring the message,”
paragraphs.simple: The weaver says it was brave of them to bring the message. She gives Annie the silk thread to say thank you.

paragraphs.context: “It is made from the cocoons of silkworms,”
paragraphs.simple: The weaver says silk comes from the cocoons of silkworms.

background.note: A silkworm makes a cocoon from one very long silk thread. People boil the cocoons and pull out the thread to make silk.

paragraphs.context: “Really? Worms? That’s neat,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks it is great that silk comes from worms. He wants to write it in his notebook.

paragraphs.context: “Please don’t!” said the silk weaver.
paragraphs.simple: The weaver stops him. How to make silk is China's most important secret. Anyone who steals it will be arrested and killed by order of the Dragon King.

background.note: For hundreds of years, only China knew how to make silk. People in other countries paid a lot of money for it. Taking silkworms out of China was against the law.

paragraphs.context: “I think you must leave quickly,”
paragraphs.simple: The weaver whispers that they must go quickly, because someone has seen them. A man is pointing at them.

paragraphs.context: “Bye!” said Annie. “Good luck on your date!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie wishes the weaver good luck when she meets the young man tonight.

paragraphs.context: They hurried away from the silk weaver.
paragraphs.simple: They leave the weaver quickly. Then someone shouts at them to stop, and Annie tells Jack to run.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran around the farmhouse.
paragraphs.simple: Behind the farmhouse is a cart pulled by oxen, full of bags of grain. Nobody is there.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked at each other, then dived into the back of the wooden cart.
paragraphs.simple: They jump into the cart and hide under the bags of grain.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s heart pounded as the shouts came closer.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's heart beats hard. He stops breathing for a moment and waits for the people to go away.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly the cart lurched forward.
paragraphs.simple: The cart suddenly moves. Someone is driving it away with them inside!

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie peeked over the bags. Jack saw the back of the driver.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are going to the city.
paragraphs.simple: They look over the bags. The driver is calmly driving the cart down the road to the walled city.

paragraphs.context: “This is great!” whispered Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they can jump out when they get into the city.

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” Jack said softly. “Then we’ll find the Imperial Library
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they will find the library and the book, then go back to the tree house. It sounds easy.
paragraphs.tone: Hopeful, but the reader guesses it will not be so easy.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath. He heard voices and the heavy tramping of feet
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears voices and the heavy sound of many feet. They look out.

paragraphs.context: A long line of men was crossing the road in front of the cart.
paragraphs.simple: A long line of men with tools crosses the road. Guards walk next to them.

paragraphs.context: He reached into his sack and pulled out the China book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes out the China book and finds a picture of the workers.

paragraphs.context: The Dragon King forced many of his subjects to start building a wall
paragraphs.simple: The Dragon King made many of his people build a wall to keep enemies out of China. Later emperors made it longer. In the end it was 3,700 miles long.

background.note: The Great Wall is many walls built over about 2,000 years. The first emperor joined older walls together. Much of the wall people visit today was built later, by the Ming emperors.
3,700 miles is about 6,000 kilometres. If you count all its parts, the Great Wall is even longer, more than 20,000 kilometres.

paragraphs.context: “Who hasn’t?” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The workers go to the wall.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says everybody has heard of the Great Wall. Those men are going to work on it now.

paragraphs.context: Just then, someone grabbed Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the driver of the cart takes hold of them and angrily asks who they are.

paragraphs.context: The man’s gaze fell on the open book in Jack’s hands.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The man is amazed by the book.
paragraphs.simple: The man sees the book. He is so surprised that his mouth opens. He lets them go and touches the book.

paragraphs.context: “It’s a book from our country,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says their books are made of paper. China invented paper, but later in the future.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Jack tells the man about his own country's future.

paragraphs.context: “Never mind,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it does not matter. Books are for reading and learning about places far away.

paragraphs.context: The man stared at them. Tears filled his eyes.
paragraphs.simple: The man looks at them and starts to cry. He loves reading and learning.

paragraphs.context: The man smiled. “You don’t understand!
paragraphs.simple: The man says he is dressed like a farmer, but really he is a scholar.

paragraphs.context: “We are great readers, learners, and writers,”
paragraphs.simple: He says scholars read, learn and write a lot. They were always the most respected people in China.

background.term: the most honored citizens in China
background.note: In ancient China, scholars who knew old books well were very respected. Later, people took hard tests about old books to get government jobs.

paragraphs.context: “But now scholars are in danger,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Now scholars are in danger, and many are hiding.

paragraphs.context: “The Dragon King is afraid of the power of our books and learning,”
paragraphs.simple: The Dragon King is afraid of books and learning. He wants people to think only his ideas. Soon he may order all the books to be burned.

background.note: In 213 B.C. the first emperor ordered many old books to be burned. Only books about medicine, farming and some other useful things were kept. Many scholars were killed.

paragraphs.context: “All the books in the Imperial Library will be burned,”
paragraphs.simple: All the library books will be burned. Annie says this is very bad and unfair.

paragraphs.context: “Listen, we have a mission to get a book from that library,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells the scholar that they must get a book from the library.

paragraphs.context: She reached into her shirt pocket as Jack reached into his sack.
paragraphs.simple: They take out their secret library cards. The letters shine in the sun.

paragraphs.context: “You are Master Librarians,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar is surprised. He has never met such young Master Librarians. He bows to show respect.

paragraphs.context: They bowed back to him.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie bow back to him, to be polite.

background.note: In China and other countries in East Asia, people bowed to show respect, like a handshake today.

paragraphs.context: He held out Morgan’s bamboo strip to the scholar.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shows the scholar the bamboo strip with the title of the story.

paragraphs.context: “We will go to the Imperial Library,” said the scholar.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar will take them to the library. He knows the story well. It is true and was written not long ago. But it will be very dangerous.

paragraphs.context: “I am happy to be doing something I believe in again,”
paragraphs.simple: The scholar is glad to do something good and right again.

paragraphs.context: They all climbed into the front of the cart.
paragraphs.simple: They sit in the front of the cart. Far away, the wall builders are marching. The oxen start to walk.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, sure, there’s a library in every town,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says every town in his country has a library. There are thousands of libraries.

paragraphs.context: “And millions of books,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie adds that there are millions of books, and nobody burns them.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Jack. “Everyone gets to go to school
paragraphs.simple: Jack says every child can go to school and learn to read.

paragraphs.context: The scholar stared at him and shook his head.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar cannot believe it. He says it sounds like a perfect place.
paragraphs.tone: Moving: for the scholar, a land of free books is a dream.

paragraphs.context: The oxcart bumped across the wooden bridge that crossed over a moat.
paragraphs.simple: The cart goes over a bridge across a moat (a wide ditch of water) and past guards at big wooden gates.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, yes, every day at sunset,” said the scholar.
paragraphs.simple: Every day at sunset a gong is hit, the gates close, the bridge goes up, and nobody can go in or out all night.

background.note: In old Chinese cities, drums and bells or gongs in towers told people the time. At night the city gates were closed.

paragraphs.context: “I guess visitors have to leave before that happens,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie guesses that visitors must leave before sunset, or they will be stuck in the city all night. This is important later.

paragraphs.context: Rows of small houses were bunched together
paragraphs.simple: Small houses of mud with straw roofs stand close together. People cook outside and wash clothes in wooden tubs.

paragraphs.context: As the oxcart bumped along, the houses got larger.
paragraphs.simple: Further in, the houses are bigger, made of painted wood and pottery tiles. They all have curved roofs.

paragraphs.context: “To keep away the bad spirits,” said the scholar.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar says curved roofs keep bad spirits away.

background.note: People in old China believed that bad spirits could only move in straight lines, so curves, bent paths and screens kept them out. Curved roofs also throw rain water away from the house.

paragraphs.context: “The spirits can only travel in straight lines,”
paragraphs.simple: The spirits can only go in straight lines, so they cannot follow a curved roof.

paragraphs.context: The cart went by some open tea shops.
paragraphs.simple: They pass tea shops and a big market. People buy and sell fish, chickens, firewood, wheels, silk, furs and jade jewelry.

background.note: Jade is a hard green stone. In China it has been loved for thousands of years, and people believed it brought good luck.
People in China have drunk tea for thousands of years. Tea houses were places to meet friends.

paragraphs.context: Some people were lined up at a stall filled with tiny cages.
paragraphs.simple: Some people stand in a line at a stall with many tiny cages.

paragraphs.context: “Crickets,” the scholar said.
paragraphs.simple: The cages hold crickets. People keep them as pets, feed them tea leaves and enjoy their soft song.

background.note: In China, people have kept crickets as pets for a very long time, for their song. Some people even had cricket fights.

paragraphs.context: The cart moved on toward the Dragon King’s walled palace.
paragraphs.simple: The cart goes to the palace, which also has walls. They stop at the gates.

paragraphs.context: “Grain delivery!” the scholar shouted up to the guard at the tower.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar says he is bringing grain, so the guard lets them in. Inside are gardens and big hills of earth with a low wall around them.

paragraphs.context: “That is the Imperial Burial Grounds,” said the scholar
paragraphs.simple: The scholar says the hills are the emperor's burial grounds.

paragraphs.context: “They are the people in your family who lived before you,”
paragraphs.simple: Ancestors are family members who lived before you. One day the Dragon King will be buried there too. 300,000 workers are building his tomb.

background.note: Old history books say about 700,000 people worked on the first emperor's tomb. It took many years.

paragraphs.context: He looked over his shoulder at the burial grounds.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks back at the burial grounds. Why do they need so many workers to build one tomb?

paragraphs.context: The scholar pointed at the palace courtyard.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar points at the palace courtyard. Dark smoke is going up into the sky. There is a fire!

paragraphs.context: The scholar snapped the reins.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar shakes the reins, and the oxen run up the path. In the courtyard there are soldiers everywhere.

paragraphs.context: Some threw wood on a huge bonfire.
paragraphs.simple: Some soldiers put wood on a huge fire. Others carry bamboo strips down the stairs from the palace.

paragraphs.context: “Yes. The strips are tied together into different bundles,”
paragraphs.simple: The scholar says each bundle of tied bamboo strips is one book.

paragraphs.context: Stepping outside was a man in a rich, flowing robe and a tall hat.
paragraphs.simple: A man in an expensive, long robe and a tall hat comes out. Jack knows him at once: the Dragon King!
paragraphs.tone: Exciting and scary: the end of the chapter.

paragraphs.context: The Dragon King watched the bonfire as it blazed up toward the sky.
paragraphs.simple: The Dragon King watches the big fire. The air around it is hot and moves like waves. Books are piled next to the fire.

paragraphs.context: They jumped down from the cart and joined the crowd by the bonfire.
paragraphs.simple: They get down from the cart and stand with the people near the fire.

paragraphs.context: The Dragon King shouted to the soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: The Dragon King shouts, and the soldiers throw the books into the fire. The bamboo makes cracking sounds as it burns.

paragraphs.context: “Stop!” she shouted again.
paragraphs.simple: Annie shouts again, but nobody can hear her because the fire is so loud.

paragraphs.context: He pointed to a bamboo book that had fallen off a waiting stack.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar points to a bamboo book that has fallen from a pile. It is their story!

paragraphs.context: But she had already snatched up the bundle of bamboo strips
paragraphs.simple: Annie quickly picks up the book and runs back.

paragraphs.context: Jack put the bundle of bamboo strips in his sack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the book in his sack. He looks around and sees the Dragon King looking at them angrily. The king comes toward them.

paragraphs.context: “Run through the burial grounds!” the scholar said to Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The scholar tells them to run through the burial grounds. The soldiers are afraid of the spirits there.

background.term: They fear the spirits of the ancestors
background.note: In ancient China, people honored the spirits of their dead family members and were afraid to make them angry.

paragraphs.context: Then she and Jack took off.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie run away fast. Soldiers shout, and an arrow flies past them.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly arrows filled the air around them.
paragraphs.simple: Many arrows fly around them. Archers are shooting from the tower!

paragraphs.context: There was a doorway in one of the mounds.
paragraphs.simple: There is a door in one of the hills, and they quickly go inside.

paragraphs.context: They were in a long hall lit with oil lamps.
paragraphs.simple: They are in a long hall with oil lamps.

paragraphs.context: “It’s so quiet,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: It is very quiet. Annie walks down the passage and finds some steps.

paragraphs.context: “We don’t know what’s down there,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not want to go down. It is a tomb, and it is creepy.

paragraphs.context: “You might be right,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack agrees but says to go slowly. He does not want to find a dead body.

paragraphs.context: Annie started down the steep steps.
paragraphs.simple: They go down and down the steep steps. Lamps light their way.

paragraphs.context: Jack blinked. Even though oil lamps glowed everywhere
paragraphs.simple: Even with all the lamps, it is hard to see at first.

paragraphs.context: When Jack’s eyes got used to the strange light, his heart nearly stopped.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack can see, he is so afraid that his heart almost stops.

paragraphs.context: They were in a room filled with soldiers—thousands of them.
paragraphs.simple: The room is full of soldiers, thousands of them.
paragraphs.tone: A big surprise at the end of the chapter.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stood frozen.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie do not move. The soldiers do not move either.

paragraphs.context: “They’re fake,” she said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says they are not real.

paragraphs.tone: Funny: brave Annie pulls a soldier's nose.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, brother,” said Jack. He walked over to the soldier

paragraphs.context: She walked down a row between two lines of soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: Annie walks between the soldiers. Jack thinks it is spooky and wants to know what this place is.

paragraphs.simple: The Dragon King had 7,000 clay soldiers made for his tomb. "Life-size" means as big as real people. The clay was baked and painted.

background.note: Today we call them the Terracotta Army ("terracotta" means baked clay). They are near Xi'an in China. Thousands of people visit them every day.

paragraphs.context: The Dragon King hoped that the clay army would protect him after he died.
paragraphs.simple: He hoped the clay army would keep him safe after his death.

paragraphs.context: “It’s like the pyramid in ancient Egypt,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers that in Egypt a queen was buried with a boat and other things to use in the next life.

background.note: In Book 3, Mummies in the Morning, Jack and Annie visit a pyramid in ancient Egypt and meet the ghost of a queen.

paragraphs.context: “No, you come here,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks it is great: every soldier has a different face.

paragraphs.context: In the flickering lamplight, they wandered down the rows of soldiers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: No two soldiers are the same.
paragraphs.simple: In the moving light of the lamps they walk around. No two soldiers have the same nose, eyes or mouth.

background.term: No two soldiers had the same nose

paragraphs.context: “Oh, man. No wonder so many people had to work on this tomb,”

paragraphs.context: There were kneeling archers and foot soldiers dressed in red and black armor.

paragraphs.simple: They have real metal weapons: swords, knives, axes, spears, bows and arrows.

background.note: Bronze swords from the tomb are still sharp and shiny today, after more than 2,000 years.

paragraphs.context: There were even life-size wooden chariots with horses.
paragraphs.simple: There are wooden chariots with horses as big as real ones. The horses look real, with white teeth and red tongues.

paragraphs.context: He pulled out his notebook and pencil.
paragraphs.simple: Jack kneels on the brick floor and writes notes.

paragraphs.context: “I think we’re lost,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they are lost. Jack does not want to believe it.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around. All he could see were rows of soldiers.
paragraphs.simple: In front, behind, left and right, Jack sees only clay soldiers.

paragraphs.simple: The rows look the same and go on and on. Jack tries not to be too afraid.

paragraphs.context: “Forget it,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the research book cannot help. Morgan said only the old legend could save them in their darkest hour.

paragraphs.simple: Annie says it is quite dark. It is a small joke: "darkest hour" means the worst time, but the tomb is also really dark.
paragraphs.tone: A little funny, even in danger.

paragraphs.context: It does seem to be getting darker in here, thought Jack.
paragraphs.simple: The tomb is getting darker, and the air is heavier. It is hard to breathe.

paragraphs.simple: Jack holds up the bamboo book and says "Save us!"

paragraphs.context: As Jack waited, the tomb seemed unbearably quiet.
paragraphs.simple: Jack waits. The tomb is terribly quiet. He asks again, but nothing happens.

paragraphs.context: The air was growing even thicker.
paragraphs.simple: The air is heavier, the light is weaker, and the soldiers look more frightening.

paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the book into his sack and runs after Annie.

paragraphs.simple: Jack says science says this cannot happen. Annie says it is magic.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Jack always thinks like a scientist.

paragraphs.simple: The thread ends: the ball is completely unrolled.

paragraphs.simple: They run up the stairs to the hall that goes to the door of the mound.

paragraphs.simple: They walk a long way. Jack stops: this hall is longer than before.

paragraphs.context: “Me neither,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie does not remember it either. Maybe these are not the same stairs.

paragraphs.context: They started walking again. They rounded a corner and came to a door.
paragraphs.simple: They walk on, go around a corner and find a door.

paragraphs.simple: Annie opens the door slowly and looks out. She is happy.

paragraphs.context: Annie stepped into the fading daylight.
paragraphs.simple: They step out. The light of the day is going away. The sun has gone down.

paragraphs.context: They were standing outside the gate of the Dragon King’s palace.
paragraphs.simple: They are outside the palace gate. The market stalls are closing.

paragraphs.simple: A gong sounds from the tower of the city walls. The gates will close!

paragraphs.simple: Jack holds his sack tightly as they run up the street, past the market and the houses.

background.term: The Silk Weaver and the Cowherd
background.note: This is one of the most famous love stories in China. In Chinese the weaver is Zhinü and the cowherd is Niulang.

paragraphs.context: “Guess what, Morgan?” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They met the people in the legend.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they met the weaver and the cowherd and helped them meet.

paragraphs.simple: The legend says that long ago they lived in the sky. When they came to earth, they fell in love.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, I imagine so,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: The bamboo book tells about their happy time on earth. But a later legend says that when they went back to the sky, the king and queen of the skies separated them with a river of stars, the Milky Way.

background.note: The Milky Way is the band of stars you can see across the night sky. In Chinese it is called the "Silver River".

paragraphs.context: “They get back together once a year,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: The couple meet once a year. On that night birds make a bridge over the Milky Way.

background.note: They meet on the seventh day of the seventh month of the Chinese calendar. This is the Qixi Festival, sometimes called Chinese Valentine's Day.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie gazed up at the bright summer sky.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie look up at the sky for a long time.

paragraphs.context: “Go home now,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan tells them to come back in two weeks. Next they will go to Ireland, more than 1,000 years ago.

background.note: Ireland is an island west of Britain. Their next trip is Book 15, Viking Ships at Sunrise.

paragraphs.context: “I’m afraid it was a very dangerous time,” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says it was a dangerous time, because Vikings often attacked places near the sea.

background.note: The Vikings came from Norway, Denmark and Sweden. About 1,200 years ago they sailed in long ships and attacked towns and churches near the sea, like in Ireland.

paragraphs.context: “Vikings?” said Jack. He’d had enough danger to last a long time.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not want more danger for a long time.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry about it now,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan says not to worry now; they should go home and rest.

paragraphs.context: From the ground, they waved to Morgan.
paragraphs.simple: They wave to Morgan and start walking home.

paragraphs.simple: Annie imagines that the adult crickets are telling the young ones a legend.

paragraphs.context: It was their mother calling them.
paragraphs.simple: Their mother calls them home.

paragraphs.context: The spell was broken.
paragraphs.simple: The magic feeling stops. The crickets sound like ordinary crickets again.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran down their street and across their yard.
paragraphs.simple: They run home across their yard.

paragraphs.context: “We got lost in a tomb,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they got lost in a tomb and a book saved them. Mom thinks it is a game.

paragraphs.context: Their mom smiled and shook her head.
paragraphs.simple: Their mother smiles and says books are wonderful. She does not know how true this is.
paragraphs.tone: Funny and warm: Mom is right in a way she does not know.

paragraphs.context: 1. Chinese writing has over 50,000 characters.
paragraphs.simple: Chinese writing has more than 50,000 characters. A legend says the first characters came from the footprints of birds and animals.

background.term: the first characters were devised from the tracks of birds and animals
background.note: The legend says a man called Cangjie made the first characters after he looked at animal footprints.

paragraphs.context: 2. In 221 B.C., China was divided into many kingdoms.
paragraphs.simple: Before 221 B.C. China had many small kingdoms. The first emperor, Shi Huangdi, made them one country. He thought scholars were dangerous, so he burned their books.

background.note: Today his name is usually written Qin Shi Huang. "Huangdi" means emperor. He gave China one kind of writing, money and measures.
B.C. means "before Christ": years counted back before the year 1. 221 B.C. is about 2,200 years ago.

paragraphs.context: 3. Silk thread comes from the cocoon of the silkworm
paragraphs.simple: Silkworms eat mulberry leaves and make cocoons of silk thread. China kept silk a secret because it sold silk to other countries.

background.note: Silk was sold along the Silk Road, a long trade route from China to the Middle East and Europe.

paragraphs.context: 4. The first emperor built the Great Wall
paragraphs.simple: The emperor built the wall to keep out enemies from the north. A legend says the wall is a dragon turned to stone.

paragraphs.context: 5. Since the 1970s, archaeologists have been investigating
paragraphs.simple: Since the 1970s, scientists have studied the tomb and dug out more than 50,000 old objects.

paragraphs.context: 6. The Chinese legend of the silk weaver and the cowherd
paragraphs.simple: The legend is connected with two stars. The weaver and the cowherd married on earth, but in heaven they were so happy that they stopped working. The king and queen of Heaven were angry and put the Milky Way between them. Once a year, magpies make a bridge so they can meet.

background.note: Vega and Altair are two bright stars on the two sides of the Milky Way. In summer you can see them high in the night sky.
Magpies are black and white birds. In China the magpie is a bird of happiness and good news.

all my best.meaning: A friendly way to end a letter, like "Best wishes".
all my best.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

all you have to do.meaning: "All they had to do was ..." means the only thing they needed to do was ... (so it was easy).
all you have to do.example: All they had to do was point to a picture and wish to go there.
all you have to do.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

along the way.meaning: While going somewhere or doing something; during a trip.
along the way.example: Along the way, they discovered that the tree house belongs to Morgan le Fay.
along the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

any day.meaning: Very soon; maybe on any day from now.
any day.example: Any day he may order the burning of the books!
any day.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

as for.example: As for the story, I know it well.
as for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at once.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be in for.meaning: "What are we in for?" means "What (hard or surprising) thing is going to happen to us?"
be in for.example: What are we in for today?
be in for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

believe in.meaning: To believe in something means to think that it is good and right (or real).
believe in.example: I am happy to be doing something I believe in again,
believe in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

breathe a sigh of relief.meaning: To breathe out loudly because you feel happy that something bad has ended.
forms: breathed a huge sigh of relief
breathe a sigh of relief.example: Jack breathed a huge sigh of relief.
breathe a sigh of relief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

bring out.meaning: To take something out so people can see it.
bring out.example: They brought out the secret library cards.
bring out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by the time.meaning: "By the time they reached the tree" means at the moment when they reached it (and not before).
by the time.example: By the time they reached their tree
by the time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch your breath.meaning: To rest until you can breathe normally again, after running.
catch your breath.example: stood still for a moment and caught their breath.
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come on.meaning: "Come on!" means "Hurry!", "Let's go!" or "Please do it!"
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

come to a halt.example: The cart slowly came to a halt.
come to a halt.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do a good job.example: “They really did a good job,” said Annie.
do a good job.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

do someone a favor.meaning: To help someone. "Can you do me a favor?" means "Can you help me?"
do someone a favor.example: “Can you do me a great favor?”
do someone a favor.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

don't worry about it.meaning: "Don't worry about it" means "Do not think about it now; it is OK."
don't worry about it.example: “Don’t worry about it now,” said Morgan.
don't worry about it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

excuse me.meaning: A polite way to start talking to someone you do not know, or to say sorry.
excuse me.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fall in love.example: When they came to earth, they fell in love.
fall in love.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fall off.meaning: To drop from something to the ground.
fall off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it or find the answer.
figure out.example: I couldn’t figure out what period of history they should visit.
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find out.meaning: To learn a fact that you did not know.
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

for sale.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for sure.example: “Now we know one thing for sure.”
for sure.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

forget it.meaning: "Forget it" means "Stop; do not do that, it will not help."
forget it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get back together.meaning: To be together again after being apart.
get back together.example: “They get back together once a year,”
get back together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get out of here.meaning: "Let's get out of here!" means "Let's leave this place now!"
get out of here.example: “Let’s get out of here!” he said.
get out of here.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get to.meaning: 1. "Everyone gets to go to school" means everyone is allowed to (has the chance to) go to school. 2. To arrive at a place ("As they got to the edge of the woods").
get to.example: Everyone gets to go to school to learn to read them.
get to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get together.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get used to.meaning: To become comfortable with something new, so that it is not strange any more.
get used to.example: When Jack’s eyes got used to the strange light
get used to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go down.meaning: To move to a lower place. When the sun goes down, it goes below the land and night comes.
go down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go into hiding.meaning: To go to a secret place so that no one can find you.
go into hiding.example: many of us have gone into hiding.
go into hiding.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go off.meaning: When a bomb or a volcano goes off, it explodes or erupts suddenly.
go off.example: Pompeii looked peaceful before the volcano went off.
go off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

guess what.meaning: "Guess what?" is a way to start telling someone surprising news.
guess what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

had better.meaning: "We'd better go" means we should go, or something bad may happen.
had better.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

have had enough.meaning: "He'd had enough danger" means he did not want any more danger.
have had enough.example: He’d had enough danger to last a long time.
have had enough.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

have on.meaning: To wear. "They had on baggy pants" means they were wearing baggy pants.
have on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hear of.meaning: To know that someone or something exists, because someone has told you about it.
hear of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand forward with something in it, to show it or give it.
hold out.example: He held out Morgan’s bamboo strip to the scholar.
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold up.meaning: To lift something and hold it high, so people can see it.
hold up.example: She held up a long, thin strip of wood.
hold up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a short time, often because you are afraid or excited.
hold your breath.example: He held his breath and waited for the people to leave.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

i'm afraid.meaning: "I'm afraid ..." is a polite way to say something sad or bad: "I am sorry to say ..."
i'm afraid.example: But I’m afraid a later legend tells us
i'm afraid.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

if only.meaning: "If only ..." means "I wish ..." (but it is not true).
if only.example: “If only she knew we aren’t pretending,”
if only.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in fact.meaning: Really; the truth is. People say "in fact" to add something more surprising.
in fact.example: In fact, there are probably thousands of libraries in our country.
in fact.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in sight.meaning: Where you can see it. "No one in sight" means you cannot see anyone.
in sight.example: There was no one in sight.
in sight.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.meaning: Far away, but you can still see or hear it.
in the distance.example: The long line of wall builders was marching in the distance.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in truth.example: “But in truth, I am a scholar!”
in truth.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

just then.example: Just then, someone grabbed Jack and Annie.
just then.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep away.meaning: To make something stay far from you.
keep away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep your head down.meaning: To keep your head low and not look up, so people do not notice you.
keep your head down.example: remember to keep your head down so no one will notice us.
keep your head down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let go of.meaning: To stop holding someone or something.
let go of.example: He let go of Jack and Annie.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

line up.meaning: To stand in a line, one person behind another.
line up.example: Some people were lined up at a stall
line up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look around.meaning: To look at the things or places around you, often to find something.
look around.example: Jack looked around to see if anyone was watching.
look around.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look over your shoulder.meaning: To turn your head and look behind you.
look over your shoulder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look up ("Jack looked up"). 2. To look for a fact in a book ("I'd better look this up").
look up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

made up of.meaning: "Made up of" means "made from" these parts. "Chinese writing is made up of many characters" means the characters are its parts.
made up of.example: Chinese writing is made up of many characters.
made up of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

me neither.meaning: "Me neither" means "I don't either." You say it to agree with something negative.
me neither.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

never mind.meaning: "Never mind" means "It is not important; forget it."
never mind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no longer.example: They no longer wore jeans, T-shirts, and sneakers.
no longer.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no problem.meaning: "No problem" means "Yes, I can do it easily" or "It is OK."
no problem.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no wonder.meaning: "No wonder ..." means "It is not surprising that ..."
no wonder.example: No wonder so many people had to work on this tomb
no wonder.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

nothing but.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

of course.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, brother.meaning: What you say when you feel a little tired of something or a little annoyed. It is not about a real brother.

oh, man.meaning: What you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. It is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a man.

on either side.example: bunched together on either side of the street.
on either side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on the way back.example: “Let’s do that on our way back,”
on the way back.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

on the way to.example: They were on their way to the walled city!
on the way to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

once a year.example: “They get back together once a year,”
once a year.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

one last time.example: Jack looked out one last time at the Chinese couple.
one last time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of breath.meaning: Breathing very hard after running, so you cannot speak easily.
out of breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pass down.meaning: To give stories, things or knowledge to younger people in your family.
pass down.example: A legend passed down from their ancestors,
pass down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up.meaning: To take something in your hand and lift it.
pick up.example: picked up a ball of yellow thread
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

plain old.example: just plain old cricket sounds again.
plain old.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull away.meaning: To move your body away from someone who is holding you.
pull away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull on.meaning: To put on clothes or a bag, often quickly.
pull on.example: Jack pulled on his pack and followed her.
pull on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull out.meaning: To take something out of a bag, pocket or other place.
pull out.example: From the folds of her robe, she pulled out a book.
pull out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

put down.meaning: To put something on the floor or on a table.
put down.example: He put down his sack and pulled out the China book.
put down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put to death.meaning: To kill someone as a punishment. "Have him put to death" means order people to kill him.
put to death.example: The Dragon King will have him put to death.
put to death.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

reach out.meaning: To move your hand forward to touch or take something.
reach out.example: Slowly he reached out and touched the book.
reach out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

see you.meaning: A friendly way to say goodbye. "See you in two weeks" means "Goodbye; we will meet again in two weeks."
see you.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake your head.meaning: To move your head from side to side, to say "no" or to show that you are sad or surprised.
shake your head.example: The young man shook his head.
shake your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

snatch up.meaning: To pick something up very quickly.
snatch up.example: she had already snatched up the bundle of bamboo strips
snatch up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

so what.meaning: "So what?" means "Why is that important?" or "I don't care."
so what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stand for.meaning: If a letter or a sign stands for something, it means that thing.
stand for.example: Each one stands for a different thing or idea.
stand for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

stretch out.meaning: To go on for a long way.
stretch out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stumble across.meaning: To find something by chance, when you were not looking for it.
stumble across.example: I stumbled across some amazing information.
stumble across.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

stumble upon.meaning: To find something by chance, often something you did not want to find.
stumble upon.example: He didn’t want to stumble upon a dead body.
stumble upon.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm before something hard.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take a look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take care of.meaning: To look after someone or something.
take care of.example: the man who takes care of the cows!
take care of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take notes.meaning: To write down short facts, so that you can remember them.
take notes.example: I spent days reading and taking notes.
take notes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: To leave or run away suddenly and fast.
take off.example: Then she and Jack took off.
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

thanks for everything.meaning: A way to thank someone for all the things they did for you.
thanks for everything.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

the way out.meaning: The door or road that takes you out of a place.
the way out.example: “Maybe it’s the way out of here.”
the way out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something else.
turn into.example: The cloth sack had turned back into his backpack.
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

watch over.meaning: To look after someone or something and keep them safe.
watch over.example: a young man stood watching over them
watch over.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what if.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

what's going on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

whatever you do.meaning: "Whatever you do, ..." means "It is very important that you ..."
whatever you do.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

wish someone luck.meaning: To say that you hope someone will have good luck. "Wish us luck" means "Say good luck to us."
wish someone luck.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

write down.meaning: To write something on paper so that you remember it.
write down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

yeah, sure.meaning: It can mean "Yes, of course." But said like this, it often means the opposite: "I don't believe you."

you know what.meaning: "You know what?" is a way to start telling someone something interesting.
you know what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

your darkest hour.meaning: "Your darkest hour" is the worst, most dangerous time for you.
your darkest hour.example: in your darkest hour, only the old legend can save you.
your darkest hour.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

your gaze falls on.meaning: "His gaze fell on the book" means he suddenly looked at the book.
your gaze falls on.example: The man’s gaze fell on the open book in Jack’s hands.
your gaze falls on.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

your mouth drops open.meaning: Your mouth opens wide because you are very surprised.
your mouth drops open.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
